doc.title: Nat Hentoff interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Trad jazz, New Orleans brass bands and Ellington on categories
summary: Trad jazz is no longer hip, but brass bands thrill; Ellington taught him not to get caught in a category.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: That’s a nice story. This morning I attended a little clinic that was entitled “Trad Jazz Alive and Well.” And I think some of the people on the panel, who I don’t think thought of that title, they were a little bit like wearing their tongues in their cheek. We talked about it a little bit, but do you think trad jazz suffers from some kind of identity —

Yeah it’s not hip anymore. It’s square. But if you listen to, and there’s still some in New Orleans, these New Orleans brass bands. There’s nothing more thrilling than a real New Orleans brass band and some of these people can still play that. But Wycliffe Gordon, when he has a chance, he can sit in with anybody, but if he sits in with some of these players who still can play Dixieland, that’s still exciting stuff. I mean Bach is not out of fashion if you like classical music. There shouldn’t be — I mean you talked about my rabbis, musicians, when I was growing up — Ellington taught me something very important. He said to me one day never get yourself caught in a category. I heard somebody on the radio talk about modern jazz. He said I heard some of those things in the twenties, some cats were doing that. You don’t listen for the genres and styles, you listen for individuals. And I’ve been doing that ever since.
